prompt.context: Your client is Jazz at Lincoln Center (JALC), a leading not-for-profit arts organization in New York City. Under the artistic direction of Wynton Marsalis, JALC is committed to providing top-quality jazz performance and education. JALC has been in existence for 25 years. Until 2003, it was housed in the Lincoln Center Complex alongside the Metropolitan Opera, NYC Ballet, and Juilliard. In 2004 JALC moved to the Time Warner Center on Columbus Circle, gaining state-of-the-art facilities, greater capacity (from 3,000 to 4,000 seats), and venues with Central Park views. JALC receives three primary revenue streams: subscriptions, single ticket sales, and donations. The general rule of thumb is that 50% of tickets should be sold to subscribers and 50% to single ticket holders. In response to significantly higher fixed costs at the new venue, JALC raised ticket prices an average of 75%. Although attendance has been up since the move, subscription rates have declined in each of the first two years in the new venue.
prompt.question: You have been hired by JALC's Director of Marketing to assist in boosting subscription rates. Brainstorm the key issues and potential drivers behind the decline in subscriptions.

clarifying_info.q: What was the average subscriber attrition rate before the move?
clarifying_info.a: From 1993 to 2003, JALC had an average subscriber attrition rate of 10%. Over that period, JALC maintained subscriptions at 50% of house capacity.

clarifying_info.q: What were the fixed costs associated with the move?
clarifying_info.a: Fixed costs (rent, utilities, etc.) increased significantly enough that ticket prices had to be raised an average of 75%.

clarifying_info.q: Has overall attendance changed since the move?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, overall attendance has been up since the move, but subscription rates specifically have declined in each of the first two years.

exhibits.title: JALC Subscriber Data 2003-2005
exhibits.shows: A stacked bar chart showing total number of subscribers for years 2003, 2004, and 2005, broken down by subscriber cohort: those who subscribed in 2003 and before, those who subscribed in 2004, and those who subscribed in 2005.
exhibits.data: 2003: ~1,400 total (all from 2003-and-prior cohort); 2004: ~1,250 total (roughly ~600 from 2003-and-prior, ~650 new 2004 subscribers); 2005: ~1,400 total (roughly ~420 from 2003-and-prior, ~600 from 2004 cohort, ~425 new 2005 subscribers)

framework: Internal – Pricing: 75% price increase likely exceeds willingness to pay; examine impact on margins vs. old scheme; explore lowering prices or boosting perceived value through subscriber perks
Internal – Product: Assess whether new venue attracts same caliber performers; evaluate comfort, location, and amenity changes; identify all ancillary offerings (drinks, merchandise, parking)
Internal – Promotion: Evaluate whether advertising is consistent with new location and brand; assess effectiveness of PR leverage
Internal – Customers: Conduct marketing research to understand why old subscribers are leaving and why single tickets are preferred over subscriptions
Internal – Company: Examine whether fixed costs can be reduced
External – Competition: Identify new competitors or substitutes created by the move; assess how existing competitors responded

External – Macroeconomic: Assess whether jazz as a genre retains audience appeal; evaluate impact of economic conditions on discretionary spending; consider tourism trends and any regulatory changes from the move

questions.prompt: Look at Figure 1 (Exhibit 1). The Director of Marketing argues this data proves JALC needs to reduce prices. Do you agree? What does the data tell you, and what do you project for 2006?
questions.guidance: Strong answer identifies the composition shift: pre-2004 the ratio was 90% resubscribers / 10% new; in 2004 it shifted to ~50/50; in 2005 to ~70/30. The new 2004 subscribers largely resubscribed in 2005 (with 10% attrition) – a positive signal. The data does not necessarily prove a price cut is required; it shows subscriber churn among legacy subscribers offset by new subscriber acquisition. Candidate should project 2006 by cohort and state assumptions explicitly.

math.setup: Break 2006 subscribers into four cohorts using 10% attrition on each prior-year cohort and estimate new subscribers from trend.
steps: New 2006 subscribers: trend shows 650 (2004) → 425 (2005) → estimate ~200 new (conservative); could be up to 425 given ongoing PR buzz

questions.prompt: The Director says: 'If we grow our subscriber base by 10% a year, how long until JALC is at capacity with subscribers?'
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize this as a Rule of 72 problem (or solve via logarithms). Must identify current subscribers (~1,400) and capacity (4,000 seats with the 50% rule implying ~2,000 subscriber seats, but the case frames it as 4,000 total capacity). Using 1,400 growing to 4,000 at 10% CAGR.

math.setup: Use Rule of 72: at 10% growth, population doubles every ~7 years. Starting at 1,400 subscribers, target is 4,000 (full house). Exact: solve 1400 × (1.1)^N = 4000, i.e., N = ln(4000/1400) / ln(1.1) = ln(2.857) / ln(1.1).
steps: Rule of 72 approximation: doubles every 7 years; 1,400 → 2,800 in 7 years → 5,600 in 14 years; capacity hit between 7 and 14 years
Exact calculation: N = ln(2.857) / ln(1.1) = 1.0498 / 0.09531 ≈ 10.6 years
math.answer: Approximately 10-11 years (Rule of 72 gives ~10.6 years exact)

brainstorming.prompt: What are all the potential reasons subscribers are leaving and what actions could JALC take to reverse the decline?

categories.name: Pricing
ideas: 75% price increase likely exceeded willingness to pay for many existing subscribers
Consider tiered subscription packages at different price points
Offer early-bird renewal discounts to retain existing subscribers
Explore value-add perks (preferred seating, backstage events, merchandise) to justify higher prices without cutting revenue

categories.name: Product / Venue
ideas: New venue may attract different (less loyal) audience than Lincoln Center
Comfort, acoustics, or ambiance may differ from old venue
Location change affects commute/convenience for legacy subscribers
New venue may attract higher-end but less jazz-devoted patrons

categories.name: Promotion & Marketing
ideas: Advertising may not be reaching legacy subscriber base
Opportunity to leverage PR buzz from new venue to attract new high-value subscribers
Target corporate sponsors at Time Warner Center for bulk subscriptions
Use digital/social channels to reach younger demographics

categories.name: Customer Understanding
ideas: Survey departing subscribers to identify specific pain points
Understand why single tickets are preferred (flexibility, price uncertainty, trial before commitment)
Segment customers: core jazz fans vs. casual attendees vs. tourists
Identify what would convert single-ticket buyers into subscribers

categories.name: Competition & Alternatives
ideas: New venue in a commercial complex creates more nearby entertainment alternatives
Lincoln Center complex still exists and offers competing performing arts
Streaming and digital jazz consumption may reduce live attendance motivation

categories.name: Macroeconomic
ideas: General economic downturn reduces discretionary spending on subscriptions
Post-9/11 tourism recovery affects NYC entertainment attendance
Any new taxes or zoning regulations from the move to Time Warner Center

recommendation: JALC's subscription decline is primarily driven by legacy subscriber attrition following the 75% price increase, not a failure to attract new audiences — new subscriber cohorts are growing and showing healthy renewal rates

Do not simply cut prices across the board; instead, introduce tiered subscription packages and enhanced subscriber value (perks, priority access, events) to retain high-value patrons while making entry-level subscriptions accessible
Invest in targeted marketing research to understand legacy subscriber attrition and design win-back campaigns
risks: Lowering prices may reduce revenue and exacerbate cash flow challenges given elevated fixed costs at the new venue
New subscriber cohorts may be less loyal than legacy base; retention must be measured over multiple years
Macroeconomic headwinds could suppress both new and renewal subscriptions regardless of pricing strategy
next_steps: Conduct subscriber exit surveys to quantify price sensitivity vs. other attrition drivers
Model revenue scenarios for tiered pricing vs. status quo
Develop subscriber loyalty program with differentiated perks
Analyze corporate subscription opportunities at Time Warner Center
Track 2006 new subscriber acquisition to validate trend projections
